How it works

Your systems fill the site. Automatically.

A small program runs on a Windows machine at Fine Vines. On demand and every night, it reads your live catalog, enriches it, and publishes the finished site. No servers to babysit, no manual copy-paste.

Step 1 · Pull

Salesforce

Reads every wine that qualifies for the web — in stock, and not a non-catalog SKU.Automatic

Step 2 · Enrich

Descriptions & images

Adds tasting descriptions, sommelier notes, and a label image for each wine.AI-assisted

Step 3 · Build

The website

Generates a fast, standalone page for every wine, plus search, news and sitemaps.Automatic

Step 4 · Publish

Bunny.net

Uploads only what changed and refreshes the live site worldwide in seconds.Automatic

Runs on demand whenever you want an update, and automatically each night. New wines appear on their own; sold-out wines drop off — no one has to remember to do it.

Built to be found

Great for Google SEO — and for AI SEO

This is the heart of the rebuild. Because every page is delivered as clean, complete HTML — not assembled in the browser like the current file — both search engines and AI assistants can read it perfectly. That’s the difference between being online and being found.

Google SEO

Every wine is its own indexable page

Thousands of pages, each with a unique title, description, and structured “Product” data, plus an auto-generated sitemap. That’s how you win searches like “Barolo Cannubi 2018 Illinois distributor.”

Where you stand in Google

A quick look: today vs. what this unlocks

We actually checked. Your live site, finevines.com, is already in Google — homepage, portfolio, about, news, plus producer and individual-wine pages. So the problem isn’t visibility. It’s two other things. First, the current wine listing is painfully slow — it often crawls, and sometimes won’t load at all, which costs you buyers and rankings alike. Second, the beautiful rebuild, shipped as it stands today, would erase that Google footprint entirely.

What “the prototype alone” means below

The new design you’ve seen is, right now, a single JavaScript file that assembles itself in the browser. Search engines can’t read that — so launching it as-is would quietly wipe out the Google presence you have today. Pre-rendering every page (this system) is exactly what prevents that and fixes the speed problem.

Wine data & label images

Our approach — and the assumptions to confirm

Getting a great-looking, well-described page for thousands of wines is the interesting challenge. Here’s exactly how we plan to handle it, stated plainly so you can sign off with eyes open.

Descriptions & sommelier notes

For wines that lack rich copy in Salesforce, we generate a tasting description and sommelier-style notes with AI, grounded in the real facts we have (producer, region, varietal, vintage, style). You can review, edit, or lock any of it.

Label & bottle images

We don’t scrape random photos off the web. The enrichment step generates each wine’s image from its own details: Claude writes a tailored prompt per wine, an image model (the kind behind ChatGPT) renders a photorealistic bottle, and a deterministic vector-label engine is always there as the guaranteed fallback. Every wine ends up with a finished, on-brand image — nothing shows a broken tile — and official producer photography drops straight in whenever you have it. Pouring elegance with a sommelier’s touch, right down to the label.

A wine for a Burgundy man

Give it a name; it returns a finished bottle

Hand the generator nothing but a name and a few details and it produces a complete, photorealistic bottle — engraved label, foil capsule, the works. Here it is for George Molitor.

By request · for a Burgundy man

A wine for George Molitor

Handed a name and a hint of pedigree, the generator returns a finished, three-dimensional bottle ready for the site. For George we didn’t reach for a table wine — this is a La Tâche Grand Cru Monopole, 1990: Vosne-Romanée at the very summit of Burgundy, in a legendary vintage. Moulded glass, foil capsule, engraved estate label.

If we’re going to invent a cellar for a man who knows French wine, we’re going to invent the good stuff.

Ten looks from one name

One generator, a whole design system

The label engine isn’t a single template. To show its range we handed it the names of your own team — ten people, ten different treatments: classic château, noir prestige, art-deco, minimalist, heraldic, rosé, champagne and more, each fully branded to the wine. In production it picks a treatment that suits each wine’s region, colour and style.

One label for every member of the Fine Vines team — pure generated artwork from a single name, no stock images and no designer.

Assumptions we need you to confirm

1. Imagery is generated, not scraped. Every wine’s bottle image is generated from its own data — an AI-rendered bottle with the vector label engine as a guaranteed fallback — so there are no stock-photo licensing worries and never a broken tile. Official producer photos swap in whenever you have them. Confirm you’re comfortable leading with generated imagery.

2. QuickBooks is the source of truth for the catalog and inventory. Because QuickBooks already syncs to Salesforce, the sync program reads the wine data from that existing synced layer — no new QuickBooks integration to build.

3. Web-eligibility rule: a wine appears on the site when it’s in stock and its Salesforce SKU does not start with 9. Confirm this is correct.

How you stack up

What the rest of Chicagoland’s sites don’t do

We looked at the field — Louis Glunz, Candid Wines, Cream Wine and the broader Chicago distributor directories. The pattern is clear: most are handsome brochure sites (several on Wix) with no searchable catalog on their own domain. The real, filterable catalog is rented from SevenFifty / Provi — a shared B2B marketplace where a distributor is one vendor among hundreds and earns no search credit for its own site.
